title: The Perseid meteors
hook: in August the Perseids streak across the northern sky

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Zhongqiu, the mid-autumn moon, and your line was the full moon together. Tonight the sky moves faster than the moon ever does.

Lying on your back in the grass at midnight is a strange thing for a grown person to do. The ground is cold. Sitting up, your neck ached from craning; flat on the grass, it finally doesn't. For a long while, nothing. Then, out of the corner of your eye, a thin bright scratch across the dark, there and gone before you can point. Somebody next to you says, did you see that? In late summer, in the northern half of the world, the Perseids are the reason people lie down in fields.
screen: `FLAT ON YOUR BACK AT MIDNIGHT.` → `A BRIGHT SCRATCH ACROSS THE DARK.` → `DID YOU SEE THAT?`

segments.voice: First, what you're seeing. A shooting star isn't a star at all. Astronomers explain it as a tiny piece of dust, left behind by a comet, hitting the air so fast that it burns up in a streak of light. The earth passes through that comet's trail around the same season each year, they say, and for a stretch the sky is busy. The meteors seem to come from where the constellation Perseus stands, which is how they got their name. Second, another name. In parts of Europe the Perseids have been called the tears of Saint Lawrence, because they fall near the feast day of Lawrence, a deacon of the early church whom tradition remembers as a martyr. So the same streaks carry a Greek hero's name and a saint's tears, depending on who was looking up. Third, a psalm about names. A psalm in the Hebrew Bible goes further. In the King James words: "He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names." In the psalm, naming the lights isn't only a human habit; every one is already known by name. For people who pray the psalm, that's part of the wonder: so much light, and none of it anonymous. Fourth, the wish. Some people make a wish on a shooting star. Where that custom began isn't in today's texts. It shows a simple instinct: when something bright and brief crosses the sky, people want to answer it. A wish, a prayer, a gasp, or just a hand on the arm of the person next to you.
screen: `NOT A STAR: A SPECK OF DUST.` · `THE TEARS OF SAINT LAWRENCE.` · `HE CALLETH THEM ALL BY THEIR NAMES.` · `SOMETHING BRIGHT AND BRIEF, ANSWERED.` · then, large: `A SHOOTING STAR.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let your shoulders sink as if you were already lying in the grass. Hold the psalm's line lightly, he calleth them all by their names; shooting stars reward patience. If you pray, let the psalm be your prayer; if you don't, just wait, and watch.
Perseid meteors. Dust from a comet, burning up in our sky, named for Perseus, and called by some the tears of Saint Lawrence. Today's word.
Your line: a shooting star. There and gone, and still worth a gasp. Until next time.

howItsDone: People who watch the Perseids go somewhere dark on clear nights during the shower, lie back and let their eyes adjust; some Catholics in Europe connect the meteors with the feast of Saint Lawrence.
